title: Rising Defunct (Zombie) Process Accumulation
exclusions: Detects a host-level, nondecreasing rise in Linux zombie-process count across four observed `Splunk_TA_nix` `ps.sh` snapshots: at least ten zombies in the latest closed bucket, net growth of at least five from the first bucket, and increases in at least two of three transitions. It intentionally complements rather than duplicates UC-1.1.13: that crawl-tier rule detects a persistent count of five or more in three buckets even when the count is flat, while this walk-tier rule detects continued accumulation and does not alert on a stable high plateau. It does not prove that every process-table row was collected; identify a parent from the stock add-on feed; explain why a parent failed to wait; measure a kernel-wide process-table limit or remaining PID capacity; inspect a container PID namespace independently; observe zombies created and reaped between polls; or establish application impact, adversary activity, or regulatory compliance. The primary SPL applies no maintenance or allow-list exclusion.
evidence: After deployment, retain the versioned `linux_rising_zombie_process_accumulation_20m` saved-search definition and ACL, schedule and dispatch history, effective `ps.sh` input and add-on versions, source-health report, the four raw table snapshots, and result rows containing `first_bucket`, `last_bucket`, `observed_at`, `host`, first/current/minimum/maximum zombie counts, net growth, growth rate, transition counts, thresholds, parsed-row count, and latest zombie details. For an incident, preserve the time-matched on-host `ps` or `/proc/<pid>/status` confirmation, namespace context, identified parent, owner decision, and resolution. These artifacts show what indexed snapshots matched; this documentation-only review created no runtime evidence and does not prove source completeness, root cause, or remediation.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index with the installed `Splunk_TA_nix` search-time knowledge, index four table-formatted `sourcetype=ps` events for `host=zombie-growth-positive` in four adjacent closed five-minute buckets. Each event must have the actual `USER PID ... STAT ... COMMAND`-style header, at least one numeric healthy row, and respectively 3, 4, 7, and 10 distinct numeric PID rows whose `STAT` (or legacy `S`) begins with `Z`. Run the SPL with fixed bounds over exactly those buckets. Expect one row with `observed_buckets=4`, `first_zombie_count=3`, `current_zombie_count=10`, `net_growth=7`, `increasing_steps=3`, and `nondecreasing_steps=3`; the latest zombie-detail list must contain only the ten latest-bucket zombie rows.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run separate four-snapshot fixtures and expect zero rows for each: stable counts 12,12,12,12 (UC-1.1.13 may correctly report persistence, but this growth rule must not); counts 3,7,6,10 (a decreasing transition); counts 6,7,8,10 (net growth only four); counts 3,3,3,10 (only one increasing transition); or any sequence with one bucket absent. Also put the text `<defunct>` in a `COMMAND` whose process state is `S` and confirm it is not counted. Inspect the pipeline before the final `where` to distinguish the expected failed predicate from extraction or collection failure.

dataSources: Primary signal: `index=os sourcetype=ps` multi-line process-table snapshots emitted by the supported `ps.sh` scripted event input in the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833), collected every five minutes for this design. `multikv` expands each table event into rows. Current Linux output exposes `PID`, `STAT`, `COMMAND`, and `USER`; add-on 8.7.0+ documentation maps legacy `S` to raw `STAT` while retaining backward compatibility. Splunk supplies `_time` and `host`. The index name and five-minute interval are deployment choices, not vendor defaults. Linux `ps` and `/proc/<pid>/{stat,status}` are response-side comparison sources, not additional indexed inputs in the base rule.
app: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833), deployed to Linux collection forwarders and to the Splunk tiers that require its parsing and search-time knowledge. No custom collector, Universal Forwarder marketplace app, premium app, or HTTP Event Collector input is required.

splunkbaseApps.name: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux

spl:
index=os sourcetype=ps host=* earliest=-25m@m latest=-5m@m
| multikv
| eval process_id=tostring(coalesce(PID,pid,process_id)), process_state=trim(coalesce(STAT,S,stat)), process_name=coalesce(COMMAND,process_name,"(command unavailable)"), process_user=coalesce(USER,user,"(user unavailable)")
| where match(process_id,"^[0-9]+$") AND isnotnull(process_state)
| eval is_zombie=if(match(process_state,"^Z"),1,0), zombie_pid=if(is_zombie=1,process_id,null()), zombie_detail=if(is_zombie=1,process_name." [PID=".process_id.", USER=".process_user.", STATE=".process_state."]",null())
| stats dc(zombie_pid) as zombie_count values(zombie_detail) as zombie_processes count as parsed_process_rows by _time host
| eval observed_at=_time
| bin _time span=5m
| stats latest(zombie_count) as zombie_count latest(zombie_processes) as zombie_processes latest(parsed_process_rows) as parsed_process_rows latest(observed_at) as observed_at by _time host
| sort 0 host _time
| streamstats current=f window=1 last(zombie_count) as previous_zombie_count by host
| eval zombie_delta=if(isnotnull(previous_zombie_count),zombie_count-previous_zombie_count,null())
| eventstats count as observed_buckets min(_time) as first_bucket max(_time) as last_bucket earliest(zombie_count) as first_zombie_count latest(zombie_count) as current_zombie_count min(zombie_count) as min_zombie_count max(zombie_count) as max_zombie_count sum(eval(if(zombie_delta>0,1,0))) as increasing_steps sum(eval(if(isnotnull(zombie_delta) AND zombie_delta>=0,1,0))) as nondecreasing_steps by host
| eval current_threshold=10, net_growth_threshold=5, net_growth=current_zombie_count-first_zombie_count, growth_rate_per_minute=round(net_growth/15,2)
| where observed_buckets=4 AND last_bucket-first_bucket=900 AND nondecreasing_steps=3 AND increasing_steps>=2 AND current_zombie_count>=current_threshold AND net_growth>=net_growth_threshold AND _time=last_bucket
| rename parsed_process_rows as current_parsed_process_rows zombie_processes as current_zombie_processes
| convert ctime(first_bucket) ctime(last_bucket) ctime(observed_at)
| table first_bucket last_bucket observed_at host current_zombie_count first_zombie_count min_zombie_count max_zombie_count net_growth growth_rate_per_minute increasing_steps nondecreasing_steps current_threshold net_growth_threshold current_parsed_process_rows current_zombie_processes
| sort 0 -net_growth -current_zombie_count host
description: Reports a Linux host when four consecutive observed `ps.sh` buckets show a nondecreasing zombie count, at least two upward transitions, net growth of five or more, and at least ten zombies in the latest closed bucket. It expands table snapshots, recognizes current `STAT` and legacy `S`, counts distinct numeric PIDs per snapshot, and rejects missing or nonconsecutive buckets.
value: A rising population of terminated-but-unreaped children is stronger evidence of an active lifecycle defect than either a momentary zombie or a large stable baseline. Detecting continued growth gives Linux and application owners time to identify the responsible parent and correct its wait/reaping behavior before process-table slots are exhausted, while keeping stable persistence under UC-1.1.13 avoids duplicate alerts with conflicting semantics.
implementation: Implement UC-1.1.13 first to establish and validate the supported five-minute `ps.sh` feed. Deploy this walk-tier saved search on the same source, schedule it every five minutes on bucket boundaries, and trigger on any returned host. The initial policy requires four consecutive observed buckets, no decreasing transition, at least two increases, net growth of five, and a latest count of ten; tune only with measured host-class behavior. Confirm a result on the host with `ps` and `/proc`, identify the parent in the relevant PID namespace, and remediate the parent application rather than signaling the already terminated zombie.
visualization: Use a latest-findings table with host, first/current/minimum/maximum zombie counts, net growth, growth rate, transition counts, closed-window times, parsed-row count, and latest zombie details. Add a 24-hour five-minute line chart of zombie count by host with markers for rising-accumulation findings, plus a separate `ps` source-health panel for last event time, snapshot count, parsed-row count, duplicate inputs, and missing expected hosts. Link to UC-1.1.13's persistent-count panel and label the two conditions explicitly as `rising` and `persistent`; never chart raw `sourcetype=ps` event count as zombie count.
schema: Splunk_TA_nix table-formatted `ps` events; CIM Performance classification supplies no standard zombie-state or accumulation dataset
dataModelAcceleration: The add-on classifies `sourcetype=ps` as Performance data, but the CIM Performance model does not preserve process state, per-snapshot PID membership, table completeness, or the ordered four-bucket growth sequence. No accelerated `tstats` equivalent is claimed. A purpose-built summary would need parity tests for `PID`, `STAT`/`S`, snapshot time, host, zero-zombie snapshots, latest-bucket details, and all continuity/growth predicates before replacing the raw search.

knownFalsePositives:
A leading `Z` is a real Linux state, not a fuzzy textual match. A returned row also represents real nondecreasing counts in the indexed snapshots. A finding can nevertheless be expected, misrouted, or misleading:

1. **Approved lifecycle or fault-injection test** — A test can deliberately create unreaped children and increase their count. Confirm the exact host, application owner, test identifier, expected rate, and bounded change window. Preserve the result as test evidence; do not create a permanent fleet-wide suppression.

2. **Short-lived burst aligned with four polls** — A parent under unusual load can temporarily fall behind and later reap all children. This still satisfies the indexed rising condition, but may not require an incident if the population clears within an approved recovery objective. Compare later snapshots and application latency; do not call it false solely because the zombies disappeared before an operator connected.

3. **Container or PID-namespace mismatch** — Host `ps` sees the host namespace, while a workload operator may use inner namespace PIDs and a different apparent parent. Resolve `NSpid`/namespace and workload ownership before declaring the result stale. The base rule is host-scoped, not pod-scoped.

4. **PID reuse and changing membership** — `dc(PID)` counts concurrent zombie rows in each snapshot; it does not prove the same children persisted across snapshots. A rising count can comprise different short-lived zombies. That is acceptable for an accumulation detector, but latest `zombie_processes` is triage context rather than durable process identity.

5. **Duplicate, delayed, truncated, or locally modified `ps.sh` output** — Duplicate input stanzas, equal timestamps, lost headers, command truncation, changed columns, or forwarding delay can select a misleading latest snapshot or reduce parsed rows. Compare raw tables, effective configuration, `parsed_process_rows`, `_indextime`, and on-host `ps`. Repair source health rather than lowering growth predicates.

6. **Host identity collision or cloned forwarder state** — Two systems writing the same Splunk `host` can interleave counts into an artificial trend. Compare asset identity, forwarder GUID, source metadata, and snapshot origin. Split the identity before acting.

7. **Known defective service awaiting a controlled fix** — An accepted defect may continue to accumulate zombies until a scheduled restart or upgrade. Keep owner, ticket, risk acceptance, maximum count, and hard expiry. Stable high counts belong to UC-1.1.13; renewed growth should remain visible even during an accepted plateau.

**Safe suppression:** keep the catalogue SPL as the unfiltered base. If local policy allows notification suppression, apply a separate post-result lookup keyed by exact `host` and literal `UC-1.1.119`, with `valid_from_epoch`, `valid_until_epoch`, owner, approver, ticket, reason, and optional expected application. Reject wildcards, open-ended entries, command-substring matching, and suppression of missing buckets, extraction failures, host collisions, or source-health alerts. Retain base matches and review every exception at expiry.
mitreAttack: N/A (operational Linux process-lifecycle and capacity monitoring; no adversary behavior or intent is asserted)
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux, Splunk search/alerting, procps-ng ps, Linux /proc, and wait-system-call primary documentation; deterministic table fixtures and host-side checks specified but not executed in a live Splunk or Linux deployment; no Splunk, Linux, application, runtime, or SME sign-off

cost.search_load_notes: The five-minute ps.sh input indexes a full process table per host. The scheduled search scans twenty closed minutes, expands each table with multikv, counts PIDs per snapshot, sorts four bucket rows per host, and evaluates three deltas.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites, Linux semantics, and relationship to UC-1.1.13

Assign a Linux platform owner, application/service owner, Splunk data owner, and alert-response owner. Install a supported Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux release on the Linux collection tier and make its parsing and search-time knowledge available where searches run. Verify the installed add-on against its compatibility and upgrade guidance; Splunkbase warns that version 6.0 changed default indexes and configuration files, so upgrades require nonproduction testing. The collection identity needs the vendor-documented permissions to execute the supplied scripts and inspect processes. The search role needs read access only to the selected OS index plus permission to schedule this saved search. Restrict process command lines and exports because applications sometimes expose file paths, tenant identifiers, tokens, or other sensitive arguments in process listings.

Use the Linux state definition, not display folklore. `ps(1)` says the `s`, `state`, and `stat` fields use `Z` for a defunct or zombie process: a terminated process that has not been reaped by its parent. `STAT` can contain modifier characters after the primary state, so `^Z` is correct and `STAT="Z"` is too narrow. The word `<defunct>` can appear in display text, but command text is neither necessary nor sufficient. `/proc/<pid>/stat` field 3 records `Z`, field 4 records the parent PID, and `/proc/<pid>/status` presents `State: Z (zombie)` and `PPid` in a human-readable form.

`wait(2)` explains the lifecycle. A terminated child retains minimal kernel information so its parent can collect termination status with `wait`, `waitpid`, or `waitid`. Until it is waited for, it consumes a process-table slot. If the parent exits, the zombie is adopted by init or the nearest configured child subreaper and is normally reaped. A zombie has already terminated, so `kill -9 <zombie-pid>` is not a repair. The responsible parent must reap its children, or an owner-approved restart/upgrade of that parent may cause adoption and cleanup. Never automate parent termination or host reboot from this search.

This UC deliberately acknowledges overlap with UC-1.1.13 rather than pretending that a second threshold creates a new signal. Implement UC-1.1.13 first. It asks whether at least five zombies persisted in each of three observed buckets and can alert on a flat population. UC-1.1.119 asks a different question: is the host's population still accumulating? It requires four consecutive observed buckets, no downward transition, at least two upward transitions, net growth of five, and a latest count of ten. A stable sequence of 12,12,12,12 belongs to UC-1.1.13 and must not fire this rule. A rising sequence of 3,4,7,10 can fire this rule before meeting UC-1.1.13's three-bucket persistence condition. Route the two searches to one Linux lifecycle runbook and deduplicate incident handling by host and condition, not by silently merging their SPL.

Ten current zombies, five net growth, four buckets, and two increases are starting policy values—not Linux, procps, Splunk, or add-on limits. They express material current volume plus sustained direction without requiring every count to increase. Baseline host classes and expected child churn before changing them. High-process batch hosts may need a larger count; low-volume critical appliances may need smaller numbers. Keep a minimum absolute count so a rise from zero to five does not page merely because its percentage change is large. Keep the no-decrease predicate if the goal remains active accumulation; removing it changes the detection into net change and requires new controls and wording.

## Step 1 — Enable and qualify the supported ps.sh collection

Use the input stanza shipped in `Splunk_TA_nix/default/inputs.conf`. Copy only the `ps.sh` stanza to `Splunk_TA_nix/local/inputs.conf`; Splunk's add-on documentation explicitly says not to copy the whole default file because local settings persist across upgrades. Preserve the exact installed script path and source type, choose the deployment index, and set a measured five-minute interval. An illustrative local override is:

```ini
[script://./bin/ps.sh]
disabled = 0
interval = 300
index = os
```

`interval=300` and `index=os` are this use case's contract, not asserted vendor defaults. If local conventions use another index, change the input, SPL, role, health search, and test fixtures together. Do not rewrite `ps.sh` just to add a field; a local edit complicates support and upgrades. The add-on's troubleshooting guide documents a bounded `COMMAND` output and a procedure for length changes. Treat command text as optional triage context even if the local script is widened.

Deploy through the normal forwarder management process and inspect the effective stanza with `splunk btool inputs list --debug`. Ensure only one active `ps.sh` stanza exists per host and that its interval is really 300 seconds. The add-on documentation requires execution access for its `bin` directory and records permission failures in `splunkd.log`. Follow the vendor's supported service privilege model and the organization's host-hardening review; do not grant arbitrary script execution merely to make this input run. Record add-on, forwarder, operating-system, and procps versions for qualification.

Search `index=os sourcetype=ps earliest=-15m` and inspect raw events before enabling the alert. Each script invocation should be one multi-line aligned process table with a header. Run:

```spl
index=os sourcetype=ps earliest=-15m
| multikv
| table _time host PID STAT S COMMAND USER
```

Splunk documents `multikv` as converting each table row to a search result and deriving fields from the header. On current Linux output expect numeric `PID`, raw `STAT`, `COMMAND`, and `USER`. Add-on 8.7.0 documentation maps the old normalized `S` field to raw `STAT` and retains backward compatibility, which is why the SPL coalesces both. Verify that `STAT` values such as `S`, `R`, `D`, and `Z` survive and that trailing modifiers are retained. A row with `STAT=Z+` is a zombie because its first character is `Z`.

Compare two indexed snapshots on each supported host class with a near-simultaneous on-host command such as `ps -eo user:32,pid,ppid,stat,comm,args --sort=pid`. Allow for script execution, indexing, and search delay. Confirm numeric PIDs and zombie counts, and record command truncation differences. The stock indexed fields do not include a documented `PPID` contract; do not add `PPID` to the base SPL or evidence as though it were present. Parent identification is an on-host response action. If exact parent-at-collection evidence is mandatory, design and review a separate normalized collector instead of silently changing this source contract.

Create an independent source-health search keyed to an authoritative expected-host inventory. Report hosts without a `ps` event for more than two input intervals, duplicate events within one interval, future `_time`, excessive `_indextime-_time`, missing headers, absent numeric `PID`, absent both `STAT` and `S`, sudden parsed-row collapse, and unexpected add-on/source-type versions. A quiet growth alert is not evidence that the source is healthy. The stock table does not carry a declared row count, so even a syntactically valid event cannot prove it represents every process visible during collection; retain that limitation.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the rising-accumulation search

Save the catalogue SPL as `linux_rising_zombie_process_accumulation_20m`. Schedule it every five minutes exactly on five-minute boundaries, for example `*/5 * * * *`, and let the SPL's explicit time bounds control the data. At a 12:00 dispatch, `earliest=-25m@m latest=-5m@m` evaluates 11:35 through but not including 11:55. That produces four closed five-minute buckets whose first-to-last bucket starts span 900 seconds. The five-minute delay allows the newest eligible `ps.sh` event to arrive. Measure actual forwarding delay; if the 95th or 99th percentile exceeds five minutes, move both bounds back without changing their 20-minute width, then rerun controls. Do not extend only the earliest time because an extra bucket will make `observed_buckets=4` fail.

`multikv` expands each raw snapshot. The first `eval` coalesces current and legacy names while retaining command and user context. The numeric PID and nonnull-state filter removes table headers and malformed rows. `match(process_state,"^Z")` implements Linux semantics. `dc(zombie_pid)` counts concurrent distinct zombie PIDs in each original snapshot; raw event count would count snapshots, not processes. `values(zombie_detail)` captures only zombie rows. `parsed_process_rows` is a diagnostic count, not a completeness proof.

The first `stats ... by _time host` establishes one count per original snapshot. `bin _time span=5m` then groups by schedule bucket, and the second `stats latest(...)` keeps the latest snapshot if collection produced more than one event in a bucket. This avoids summing process rows across snapshots. Multiple snapshots are still a health anomaly: selecting latest makes the analytical rule deterministic when times differ, but equal timestamps or duplicate host identities require source repair.

After `sort 0 host _time`, `streamstats current=f window=1 last(zombie_count) by host` attaches the immediately preceding count for that host. `current=f` is essential; without it, the current row can be included and every delta can become zero. The next `eval` computes one delta for each transition. `eventstats` attaches host-level sequence facts to all four rows: observed count, first/last bucket, first/current/minimum/maximum counts, number of positive transitions, and number of nonnegative transitions.

The final predicate enforces all semantics. Four rows plus `last_bucket-first_bucket=900` proves that the observed bucket starts are consecutive. Three nondecreasing steps means no dip; two or more positive steps rejects a single late jump such as 3,3,3,10. `current_zombie_count>=10` establishes material current volume, and `net_growth>=5` rejects small drift. The result retains only the last bucket's row, so `current_zombie_processes` and `current_parsed_process_rows` describe the latest closed observation. The displayed `growth_rate_per_minute` is net count divided by the 15 minutes between first and last observation; it is a presentation aid, not an independent regression or forecast.

Trigger the scheduled alert when result count is greater than zero. Route one result per host. Prefer incident deduplication keyed by `host` and use-case ID over a long Splunk throttle: a long throttle can hide continuing growth, while every five-minute dispatch naturally re-evaluates an overlapping sequence. Include the condition name `rising` in the title so UC-1.1.13's `persistent` result is not mistaken for a duplicate search execution. If both fire, combine response under one parent incident while preserving both analytical facts.

The add-on labels `ps` as Performance data, but CIM Performance has no standard process-state sequence that reproduces this rule. Do not replace it with CPU, memory, process-start Endpoint data, `ps_metric`, or a `tstats count` and call the result equivalent. `ps_metric` is a different metrics source contract and is not used here. No `cimSpl` is supplied.

## Step 3 — Validate extraction, ordering, controls, and overlap

Build fixtures as actual table-formatted raw events, not as pre-extracted scalar fields. Table parsing is part of the control. Use the installed add-on's current Linux header and aligned columns; set each event's `host` and `_time` explicitly in an isolated index. Include at least one healthy numeric row so each snapshot remains observable when zombie count is zero or small. Use distinct numeric PIDs within each snapshot. PIDs may repeat across snapshots because the rule measures count, not identity persistence.

Execute the positive scenario at fixed closed bucket times with counts 3,4,7,10. Run the exact SPL with only index and fixed-time changes. Expect one row and assert every field named in `controlTest`. Inspect after the first `stats` to prove one count per raw event, after the second `stats` to prove one latest observation per bucket, after `streamstats` to prove deltas 1,3,3, and after `eventstats` to prove consecutive coverage and net growth. Confirm `current_zombie_processes` comes from the final bucket and contains ten entries.

Execute every negative sequence separately. Stable 12,12,12,12 is the critical overlap test: this UC must return nothing, while UC-1.1.13 can correctly report a persistent high count. The 3,7,6,10 sequence must fail `nondecreasing_steps=3`; 6,7,8,10 must fail net growth; 3,3,3,10 must fail positive-transition count; a missing bucket must fail observed count or span. Use a command containing `<defunct>` with `STAT=S` and verify it remains healthy. Test `STAT=Z+` and verify it counts. Test legacy `S=Z` with no `STAT`, a nonnumeric PID, absent header, duplicate snapshot, delayed snapshot, and two hosts interleaved before sorting.

Test exact threshold boundaries: current 9 versus 10, net growth 4 versus 5, one versus two positive transitions, and two versus three nondecreasing transitions. Test a sequence that starts at zero and ends at ten. Confirm zero-zombie snapshots survive aggregation as count zero rather than disappearing. If the installed Splunk release or add-on causes `dc` to omit an all-null group, add a healthy-row fixture and inspect the command result before changing production SPL; any change must retain zero-observation semantics and rerun all controls.

There is no separate Linux vendor UI for this kernel state. Compare with the native Linux process interface: use a near-simultaneous `ps` listing, then `/proc/<pid>/status` and `/proc/<pid>/stat` for a still-present PID. On a staging host, compare at least four successive indexed snapshots with `ps`. For any observed zombie, immediately capture `ps -o pid,ppid,user,stat,lstart,comm,args -p <pid>` and `/proc/<pid>/status` while it still exists. A process may be reaped between the snapshot and comparison, which is expected race behavior and must be recorded rather than treated as fabricated data. Where containers are involved, record host PID, namespace identifiers, and workload mapping. Confirm the Splunk `host` key maps to exactly one machine.

Measure collection interval and delay over at least a day. Use raw-event `timechart span=5m count by host` for source cadence, not zombie count. Track parsed rows per snapshot and compare with host process volume. Run the saved search on its actual cron schedule and verify the evaluated bounds from job inspection. A manually selected UI time picker can override or obscure saved bounds; use dispatch metadata when validating production scheduling.

This editorial review specifies tests but did not execute them. Keep `status=draft` until a representative Linux/add-on/Splunk matrix, fixtures, source-health search, schedule, alert action, dashboard, and response runbook have passed local validation. Do not convert documentation review into a `verified` claim.

## Step 4 — Operationalize response, evidence, and safe remediation

Build the dashboard described in `visualization`. Put source-health and expected-host coverage above findings. The rising table should show first and current count, net growth, three transition facts, latest observation time, and latest process list. Link to a 24-hour per-snapshot trend and the UC-1.1.13 persistent table. Label counts as `zombie processes in latest parsed snapshot`; do not label them dead processes, failed services, memory usage, or process-table percentage.

When a finding fires, confirm current state through the approved administration path. Run `ps -eo user:32,pid,ppid,stat,lstart,comm,args --sort=ppid,pid` and filter rows whose state starts with `Z`. For a still-present PID, inspect `/proc/<pid>/status` for `State`, `Pid`, `PPid`, and namespace identifiers. Group zombies by parent PID, then inspect each parent with `ps -p <ppid> -o pid,ppid,user,stat,lstart,comm,args`. Review service-manager status, application logs, recent deployments, worker limits, signal handling, child-exit code, container runtime context, and whether a configured subreaper owns the children.

Do not send signals to zombies expecting cleanup. They no longer execute. Ask the application owner whether the parent is expected to call a wait interface, has a broken SIGCHLD handler, stopped consuming child status, is deadlocked, or is an intentional subreaper. Correct code and upgrade are preferred. If urgent risk justifies restarting the parent, use the normal service change, dependency, availability, and rollback process. Confirm that children are adopted/reaped and that the next four snapshots stop rising. Never have Splunk kill the parent, restart a service, terminate a container, or reboot a host automatically.

Escalation should consider rate, absolute count, host process/PID limits, application criticality, inability to fork, and observed service symptoms. This search does not calculate distance to exhaustion. Ten zombies on a host with a large process limit is not proof of imminent outage, while a fast continuing rise can still demand urgent investigation. Correlate with failed fork/clone messages, service errors, latency, process count, PID namespace limits, and host capacity through separately validated sources. Do not infer CPU or memory pressure from a zombie count.

Preserve the artifacts listed in `evidence` under the operations retention policy. Restrict raw command lines and exports. A result row demonstrates that four received snapshots met the rule; it does not establish that every process was visible, that the same PIDs persisted, or that a named command was the parent. Capture the parent only from time-matched host evidence. Record when the process vanished before inspection and use application logs or controlled reproduction rather than inventing a root cause.

Use UC-1.1.13 and UC-1.1.119 as two states in one runbook. Persistent-flat may indicate a bounded but unfixed reaping defect. Rising indicates continued accumulation. A host can transition between them. Resolution requires source healthy, no continued rise across the evaluated window, and an owner disposition for any remaining persistent zombies. Closing only because this rising rule stops firing can leave a stable population that UC-1.1.13 still reports.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot source- and search-specific failures

- **No `ps` events:** verify add-on deployment, the exact `ps.sh` stanza, `disabled=0`, script/bin execution rights, service privilege model, index routing, forwarding, role access, and `ExecProcessor` or permission messages in `splunkd.log`. Do not replace the missing source with HEC or a fabricated `state` field.
- **Raw table exists but `PID`/`STAT` are null:** confirm the event uses `sourcetype=ps`, the complete header is retained, `Splunk_TA_nix` search-time knowledge is installed on the search tier, and `multikv` sees aligned columns. Compare current `STAT` with legacy `S`. Repair parsing rather than searching `_raw` for `<defunct>`.
- **Legacy `S` works but `STAT` does not:** the installed add-on/output predates or differs from the documented 8.7.0 mapping. Record the version and compatibility. The SPL supports `S`; qualify before upgrade and confirm both fields do not contain conflicting primary states.
- **Zombie count is much higher than on-host `ps`:** compare collection and response times, host identity, namespace, duplicate inputs, PID reuse, script format, and latest-per-bucket selection. Zombies can be reaped before response. A timestamp race is not permission to subtract arbitrary counts.
- **Zombie count is lower than on-host `ps`:** inspect command/table truncation, header damage, process visibility of the collector identity, `_raw`, numeric PID filtering, and event loss. The stock source has no declared completeness count; raise a source-quality issue.
- **`observed_buckets` is not four:** inspect actual interval, cron boundary, search dispatch time, delay, duplicate timestamps, and latest bound. Keep the 20-minute range and four-bucket contract aligned. Do not change `observed_buckets=4` to `>=4` without defining which four observations drive deltas.
- **Buckets are present but span is not 900 seconds:** collection or dispatch is not aligned to five-minute buckets, or an extra/missing bucket entered the range. Verify cron and time modifiers. Fixed bounds in a control test should produce starts exactly five minutes apart.
- **All deltas are zero unexpectedly:** ensure `sort 0 host _time` precedes `streamstats` and `current=f window=1` remains present. Confirm four bucket rows survive. Without `current=f`, the current count can be compared with itself.
- **One host's previous count comes from another host:** verify the `by host` clause, nonnull host metadata, sorting, and host collisions. Do not coalesce missing host to a shared placeholder.
- **Stable high hosts no longer alert here:** expected. This UC is the rising detector. Confirm UC-1.1.13 is enabled and healthy for persistent plateaus; do not weaken this rule to recreate duplicate behavior.
- **Alert repeatedly creates tickets:** deduplicate incident workflow by host/use-case condition while retaining each scheduled result. Avoid long search throttles that hide renewed growth. Link persistent and rising findings to one parent incident when appropriate.
- **Command names are clipped:** the add-on documents a command-length limit and local adjustment. Prefer PID, state, time, and on-host owner lookup; do not use truncated `COMMAND` as a globally unique suppression key.
- **`/proc/<pid>` is absent during triage:** the parent or subreaper reaped it after collection. Check the next snapshot, application logs, and incident timing. Absence now does not invalidate an earlier indexed state, but it limits parent attribution.
- **Container operator cannot find the host PID:** map host and inner PID namespaces using approved runtime tooling and `/proc` namespace fields. The base rule does not promise pod identity or inner-namespace PPID.

Apply exceptions only after the base result forms, using the exact, expiring governance described in `knownFalsePositives`. A source-health failure, missing bucket, parser defect, host collision, or unowned result is never an exception candidate. Preserve suppressed base matches so accepted defects cannot silently accelerate.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for finished programs that the server has not cleaned up and warn when their number keeps climbing. That gives the team time to fix the program responsible before the server has trouble starting new work.
